'''Malcolm Leslie Hodder Green''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS|FRSC}}<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Crabtree|first=Robert H.|date=2021|title=Malcolm L. H. Green. 16 April 1936 — 24 July 2020|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume=70|pages=175–188|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2020.0038|s2cid=231643578|doi-access=free}}</ref> (16 April 1936 &ndash; 24 July 2020)<ref>[https://www.balliol.ox.ac.uk/news/2020/july/professor-malcolm-green-1936-2020 Professor Malcolm Green 1936-2020]</ref> was Professor of [[Inorganic Chemistry]] at the [[University of Oxford]].  He made many contributions to [[organometallic chemistry]].<ref>{{cite web |publisher=University of Oxford |title=Professor M. L. H. Green |url=http://research.chem.ox.ac.uk/malcolm-green.aspx |access-date=22 August 2013 |archive-date=24 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190724091709/http://research.chem.ox.ac.uk/malcolm-green.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | author=Anon|title=Green, Prof. Malcolm Leslie Hodder | id = U18020 | year = 1986 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.18020|location=Oxford}}</ref>

==Education==
Born in [[Eastleigh]], Hampshire, he was educated at [[Denstone College]]<ref name=whoswho/> and received his [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[Acton Technical College]] (London University External Regulations) in 1956 and his PhD from [[Imperial College of Science and Technology]] in 1959 for research carried out under the supervision of [[Geoffrey Wilkinson]].

==Career==
[[File:MLHGtiag.png|thumb|left|Structure of (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)TiCl<sub>3</sub>([[dmpe]]), highlighting an [[agostic interaction]] between the methyl group and the Ti centre.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1039/dt9860001629|title=Evidence for Carbon–Hydrogen–Titanium Interactions: Synthesis and Crystal Structures of the Agostic Alkyls [TiCl<sub>3</sub>(Me<sub>2</sub>PCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>PMe<sub>2</sub>)R] (R = Et or Me)|journal=J. Chem. Soc., Dalton Trans.|year=1986|page=1629|author=Z. Dawoodi |author2=M. L. H. Green |author3=V. S. B. Mtetwa |author4=K. Prout |author5=A. J. Schultz |author6=J. M. Williams |author7=T. F. Koetzle |issue = 8|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1230034}}</ref>]]

After his PhD, Green undertook a [[postdoctoral research]] year with Wilkinson before moving to the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1960 as Assistant [[Lecturer]] and being appointed a [[Fellow]] of [[Corpus Christi College, Cambridge]] in 1961.<ref name="TelegraphObit">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=Malcolm Green, inorganic chemist whose lab was a thrilling place in which to work – obituary |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2020/09/21/malcolm-green-inorganic-chemist-whose-lab-thrilling-place-work/ |work=[[Daily Telegraph]] |date=21 September 2020 |access-date=21 September 2020}}</ref> In 1963 he was appointed a [[wikt:septcentenary|Septcentenary]] [[Fellow]] of [[Inorganic Chemistry]] at [[Balliol College, Oxford]] and a Departmental Demonstrator at the [[University of Oxford]]. In 1965, he was made a Lecturer, and he was also a [[Royal Society]] Senior [[Research Fellow]] in Oxford 1979–86. In 1989, he was appointed Professor of Inorganic Chemistry and Head of the Inorganic Chemistry Laboratory at Oxford and Fellow of [[St Catherine's College, Oxford]]. In 2004, he became an Emeritus Research Professor. He was a co-founder of the Oxford Catalysts Group plc in 2006.<ref name="TelegraphObit"/>

Green held many visiting positions including: Visiting Professor, Ecole de Chimie and Institute des Substances Naturelles, Paris (1972), [[Alfred P. Sloan]] Visiting Professor, [[Harvard University]] (1975), Sherman Fairchild Visiting Scholar at the [[California Institute of Technology]] (1981), and Walter Hieber Gastprofessor, [[LMU Munich]], Germany (1991).

== Research ==
{{Primary sources|section|date=July 2023}}
Green's earliest publications described metal-hydride and metal-olefin complexes,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Dicyclopentadienylrhenium hydride|author1=Green, M. L. H. |author2=Pratt, L. |author3=Wilkinson, G. |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society|year=1958|pages=3916–22|doi=10.1039/jr9580003916}}</ref> themes that he pursued throughout his career.  Many of his early contributions focused on the chemistry of [[molybdocene dihydride]] ((C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>MoH<sub>2</sub>) and the related tungsten derivative.  These compounds were shown to engage in many reactions related to [[C-H bond activation]].<ref name=Brook/>

With Rooney, he was an active proponent of various mechanisms to explain stereochemistry in [[Ziegler–Natta]] polymerisation. He used metal vapour synthesis, especially for the preparation of early [[metal sandwich complex]]es. He and his students synthesised several examples of complexes exhibiting [[Agostic interaction|"agostic"]] bonds.<ref name=Brook>Brookhart, M.; Green, M. L. H.; Parkin, G., "Agostic Interactions in Transition Metal Compounds", Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 2007, 104, 6908–6914.</ref> The word was suggested to him by [[Jasper Griffin]], professor of Classics at Balliol, whom Green asked for an appropriate Greek word to describe the close bonding phenomenon.  This work would later lead to the so-called "modified Green-Rooney mechanism" for Ziegler–Natta catalysis, wherein agostic interactions guide the stereochemistry of the alkene insertion step.  This proposal found wide acceptance.  His work on metal carbide catalysts led to the [[corporate spin-off]] company Oxford Catalysts plc, which became Velocys.<ref name="TelegraphObit"/>

Green along with [[Stephen G. Davies]] and [[Michael Mingos]] compiled a set of rules that summarise where [[Addition to pi ligands|nucleophilic additions]] will occur on pi ligands known as the [[Green–Davies–Mingos rules]].<ref name=DaviesGreen1978/> His former doctoral students include [[Vernon C. Gibson]].<ref name=vern>{{cite thesis|degree=DPhil|publisher=University of Oxford|url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/OXVU1:LSCOP_OX:oxfaleph016541863|title=Synthesis and reactivity studies on high-energy tertiary phosphine transition metal compounds|first= Vernon Charles|last=Gibson|date=1983|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.348027}}|website=bodleian.ox.ac.uk|oclc=59298028}}</ref>

Green developed the [[Covalent bond classification method|covalent bond classification (CBC) method]] in 1995 to describe the ligands and bonding in coordination and organometallic complexes.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1995-09-20|title=A new approach to the formal classification of covalent compounds of the elements|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0022328X9500508N|journal=Journal of Organometallic Chemistry|language=en|volume=500|issue=1–2|pages=127–148|doi=10.1016/0022-328X(95)00508-N|issn=0022-328X|last1=Green |first1=M.L.H. |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Green|first1=Malcolm L. H.|last2=Parkin|first2=Gerard|date=2014-06-10|title=Application of the Covalent Bond Classification Method for the Teaching of Inorganic Chemistry|journal=Journal of Chemical Education|volume=91|issue=6|pages=807–816|doi=10.1021/ed400504f|bibcode=2014JChEd..91..807G |issn=0021-9584}}</ref>

Towards the end of his career Green's interests shifted to include studies of carbon nanotubes, developing methods to "uncap" (open) them,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tsang |first1=S. C. |last2=Chen |first2=Y. K. |last3=Harris |first3=P. J. F. |last4=Green |first4=M. L. H. |title=A simple chemical method of opening and filling carbon nanotubes |journal=Nature |date=1994 |volume=372 |issue=6502 |pages=159–162 |doi=10.1038/372159a0 |bibcode=1994Natur.372..159T |s2cid=4348976 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/372159a0 |access-date=19 July 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and investigating their filling with metals and with salts.

==Awards and honours==
His numerous awards include: 
{{div col|colwidth=35em}}
*1972: Awarded the [[Corday-Morgan medal]] in Inorganic Chemistry by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (RSC)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/CordayMorganPrizes/PreviousWinners.asp|title=Corday-Morgan Prize Previous Winners |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|access-date= 3 May 2018}}</ref>
*1977: Medal in Transition Metal Chemistry from the RSC<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/ChemistryofTransitionMetals/PreviousWinners.asp|title=Chemistry of Transition Metals Award Previous Winners |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|access-date= 3 May 2018}}</ref>
*1982: [[Tilden Prize]] and Lectureship, RSC<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/TildenPrizes/PreviousWinners.asp|title=Tilden Prizes Previous Winners|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref>
*1984: American Chemical Society Award in Inorganic Chemistry<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-in-inorganic-chemistry.html|title=ACS Award in Inorganic Chemistry|publisher= American Chemical Society|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref> 
*1985: Elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS)<ref name=frs>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117020805/https://royalsociety.org/people/malcolm-green-11535/ |archive-date=17 November 2015 |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/malcolm-green-11535/ |location=London |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |author=Anon |year=1985 |title=Professor Malcolm Green FRS  }}</ref> 
*1985: Medal in Organometallic Chemistry, RSC<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/OrganometallicChemistryAward/Previouswinners.asp|title=Organometallic Chemistry Award Previous Winners|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref>
*1988: Sir [[Edward Frankland]] Prize Lecturership, RSC<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/FranklandAward/PreviousWinners.asp|title=Frankland Award Previous Winners|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref>
*1995: Awarded the [[Davy Medal]] by the [[Royal Society]]<ref name=frs/>
*1997: Medal in Organometallic Chemistry from the [[American Chemical Society]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-in-organometallic-chemistry.html|title=ACS Award in Organometallic Chemistry|publisher= American Chemical Society|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref> 
*1992: From the [[Gesellschaft Deutscher Chemiker]], the Karl-Ziegler Prize 
*2000: Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson Medal and Prize, RSC<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/SirGeoffreyWilkinsonAward/PreviousWinners.asp|title=Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson Award Previous Winners |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref>
* Elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (FRSC){{when|date=February 2018}}
*2015: From the [[European Association for Chemical and Molecular Sciences]], the European Prize for Organometallic Chemistry<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blogs.rsc.org/dt/2016/05/14/malcolm-green-frs-in-celebration-of-his-80th-birthday/|title=Malcolm Green FRS: In celebration of his 80th Birthday|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|year=2016|access-date=1 January 2020}}</ref>
